Our cosmic ignorance is vastly bigger than our knowledge. A quantitative manifestation of this fact is that 95% of the mass-energy budget of the Universe at the present time is of an unknown nature, whereas only 5% is ordinary matter familiar to us. Out of the 95% in invisible components, 68% is labeled `dark energy’ and 27% is labeled `dark matter’. Whereas dark matter is known to condense into halos around gravitationally-bound objects, like our own Milky-Way galaxy, dark energy is known to drive the accelerated expansion of the Universe and is assumed to be spatially uniform.

But is that really the case? Could dark energy be non-uniform? In a new paper (accessible here) that I wrote with the brilliant PhD student, Oem Trivedi, we studied the open fundamental question of whether the Universe might contain voids that are deficient in dark energy. If we happen to be embedded in such a void, the local Hubble expansion rate of the Universe would be different than its global value. Such a discrepancy could explain the difference between the expected and the measured values of the Hubble constant, known as the “Hubble tension” between measurements of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) in the early Universe and local measurements.

Motivated by the recent discovery of dark matter deficient galaxies, our new paper asks the fundamental question: Could sufficiently large regions of the Universe be deficient in dark energy as well?

We investigate this possibility by developing a phenomenological framework that distinguishes genuine dark energy deficiencies from voids of matter by following the related cosmic expansion and other observational imprints. In particular, our calculations show that a 10% deficiency in dark energy can suppress the expansion of a representative void by approximately 2.7%, generating velocity residuals of order 60 to 100 kilometers per second across scales of 100 to 150 million light years. Intriguingly, we find that deficiencies of order 20% across a billion light years, could potentially account for the observed Hubble tension. Our study identifies observational strategies with galaxy surveys (such as those obtained by DESI, Rubin, peculiar velocity surveys, and cosmic void catalogues), as a new avenue for testing whether the dark energy driving cosmic acceleration is truly uniform as commonly assumed.

The Hubble tension is an observed discrepancy between the expansion rate inferred from the local distance ladder and that inferred from the early Universe under the standard cosmological model. If dark energy deficient regions are indeed responsible for a significant part of this discrepancy, then the theoretical framework that we developed makes a concrete and falsifiable prediction: the largest nearby under-dense environments should exhibit an expansion residual that cannot be accounted for by their measured matter deficiency alone. The most compelling targets are hence the local under-dense environment surrounding us, exceptionally extended structures such as the Eridanus super-void and the largest and deepest void systems identified in surveys such as DESI. In these regions, the tests proposed in our paper should be applied jointly by modeling void expansion, peculiar velocities, density and momentum statistics, supernova distance residuals, gravitational lensing and gravitational potential evolution. For a single spherical region to explain the local Hubble tension, the same spatial configuration must reproduce the required isotropic shift in the distance scale without generating an excessive directional Hubble anisotropy or excessive dipole and quadrupole moments in the cosmic microwave background for our location. Our location within the void region would itself be a falsifiable parameter of the model rather than an arbitrary geometrical choice.

The proposed observational searches could identify coherent regions extending over a billion light years in which the inferred kinematics are consistent with a genuine dark energy deficiency, and where the characteristic deficiency potentially reaches the tens of percent level required by the Hubble tension. If the full Hubble tension is produced by one such spherical region, the same reconstruction should additionally locate us sufficiently close to its center that the predicted angular multipoles of the microwave background remain compatible with observations. Failure of this centering and anisotropy constraints would strongly disfavor the single region explanation even if dark energy deficient environments themselves were independently detected. If the same spatial profile that produces an apparent Hubble tension near the locally measured value also predicts the observed velocity residuals, momentum statistics and potential evolution without independent retuning, the case for a spatially non-uniform dark energy component would become considerably stronger. An especially compelling result would be for this same profile to satisfy the cosmic microwave background anisotropy constraints without requiring an implausibly fine-tuned observer location.

Conversely, failure to find such correlated signatures in the very environments where this mechanism requires them would directly constrain, and potentially rule out, dark energy deficiency as an explanation of the Hubble tension. The central claim of our study would be not to merely say that dark energy deficient regions may exist, but that if they are responsible for the Hubble tension, then their characteristic scale, amplitude and observational fingerprints are sufficiently specific that present and forthcoming galaxy surveys should be able to find them or decisively exclude them.

Our central result is that if dark energy deficient regions are responsible for the Hubble tension, astronomers should find a local dark energy deficient void across a billion light years with tens of percent deficit in dark energy, whose matter profile, velocity field, momentum statistics, supernova distances, and angular isotropy all agree with one common spatial solution. Failure at any one of these constraints can disprove this explanation for the Hubble tension even if regions with a milder deficiency in dark energy exist.

ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Avi Loeb is chair of the UAP Science Advisory Council to the White House, Pentagon, FBI and intelligence agencies, director of the Galileo Project, founding director of Harvard University’s — Black Hole Initiative (2016–2021), former director of the Institute for Theory and Computation at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (2005–2026), and the former chair of the astronomy department at Harvard University (2011–2020). He is a former member of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (2018–2019) and a former chair of the Board on Physics and Astronomy of the National Academies (2018–2021). He is the bestselling author of “Extraterrestrial: The First Sign of Intelligent Life Beyond Earth” and a co-author of the textbook “Life in the Cosmos”, both published in 2021. The paperback edition of his new book, titled “Interstellar”, was published in August 2024.
